text:
A: Alright? Can you hear me okay? I'm Gary.
B: Hello, yes, I can hear you very well. I am Bożena. Nice to meet you.
A: Lovely to meet you, my love. Where are you based then?
B: Southampton. Bitterne, if you know it, on the east side.
A: Oh, I know Southampton a bit. I went down the boat show years ago with a lad from work, never bought a boat mind. I'm in Bridgwater, Somerset. Born and bred, never really left, you know. How did you get on with that puzzle thing at the start? I was hopeless. I sat there turning it round like a muppet.
B: The puzzle? Erm, I think I did okay, but I check everything twice, so it took me very long time. My husband says I would check the sky is still blue.
A: Ha! No, that's good, that's proper. So what do you do then, Bożena, are you working?
B: Not at the moment, no. I was pharmacy technician, eleven years at a pharmacy in Shirley, and then the branch closed, in 2023. So, sort of, I am looking for something part-time. Maybe a GP surgery, or hospital, somewhere more steady than the high street.
A: Oh, that's a shame. Were you there long? Sorry, you just said, eleven years. That's a good stretch. You'd miss the regulars, I bet.
B: Yes, the regulars, exactly. People used to ask for me by name. "Is the Polish lady in?" I miss that more than the work, I think.
A: Funny, that, innit. I'm the same. I was nineteen years at a food depot, driving a forklift, doing the paperwork, showing the new lads round. Then my back went, a disc, and the sciatica down my leg, and I've been signed off two year now. And it's not the lifting I miss, it's the people. You'd have a laugh on nights, you know, a bacon roll at three in the morning. Anyway, sorry, I'm going off on one.
B: No, no, it's okay. I understand. When the pharmacy closed it was, erm, how you say, I felt a little bit lost.
A: Yeah. Lost, that's the word. Are you keeping busy, though?
B: Oh yes, very busy. I walk by the river every day, I help at the church coffee morning, and I am knitting a jumper for my grandson with a dinosaur on it.
A: A dinosaur! He'll love that. How old is he?
B: He is five. And my granddaughter is seven. Do you have grandchildren? I saw a little girl in a fairy costume, in your photo.
A: That's Poppy, she's four. My daughter Leanne's little one, they're over in Taunton. She stays with me some weekends, I keep the spare room made up. Her latest thing is she calls me "Grumpa" when I won't let her have another biscuit. Cheeky madam.
B: Grumpa! That is very good.
A: I'm not even grumpy, I'm a soft touch. She had her nativity at nursery at Christmas and I was a right mess, tissues out and everything. Leanne still takes the mick.
B: My daughter is a teacher, primary school, and she says the grandparents always cry at nativity. So you are normal, Gary.
A: Well, that's a relief, cheers. And what about you, do you get back to Poland much?
B: Once or twice a year. My mother is eighty-four, still in Olsztyn, and my sister looks after her. It is, erm, sometimes difficult, being so far away.
A: Yeah, I bet. My dad went at sixty-four, a stroke, so I know how you think about it, you know. You want to be near.
B: Yes. I am sorry about your father.
A: Ah, it's a long time ago now. You've got a very kind face, you know, you remind me of my sister, she's a worrier too, checks the door three times before bed.
B: Then I think I would like your sister. Is this enough talking, or should I...
A: No, you're grand, keep going, we've got ages yet, haven't we? I think...
